title: HTML: Building Blocks of the Web
summary: Write real web pages with headings, lists, links, images, forms and accessible structure.
objectives: Write elements with correct opening and closing tags
Structure a page with headings, paragraphs, lists, links and images
Build a form where every input has a label
Find and fix basic accessibility problems

lessons.title: Tags are labels on boxes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Web pages are made of labeled boxes Every web page you have ever visited is written in **HTML**. That stands for *HyperText Markup Language*. It's a long name for a simple idea: you put **labels** around your words, so the browser knows what each part is. A label in HTML is called a **tag**. Tags live inside angle brackets: `<` and `>`. Here's a heading: ```html

Welcome to my page

``` - `

` is the **opening tag**. It says "a big heading starts here." - `

` is the **closing tag**. See the slash `/`? It says "the heading ends here." - The words in the middle are the **content**. That's what people see. The opening tag, the content and the closing tag together make an **element**. > The browser never shows the tags. It reads them like secret instructions, then shows only the content. ### New words - **HTML** (*HyperText Markup Language*): the language web pages are written in. - **Browser**: the app that shows web pages, like Chrome, Safari or Edge. - **Tag**: a label in angle brackets, like `

`. - **Element**: an opening tag + content + closing tag.

lessons.title: Tags and elements
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Tags, elements and the shape of a page **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) describes the *structure* of a web page. It isn't a programming language: it has no logic or loops. It's a **markup language**, meaning you mark up plain text with tags that say what each piece is. ### Tags and elements A **tag** is a keyword in angle brackets. Most come in pairs: ```html

Welcome to my page

``` - `

` is the **opening tag**; `

` is the **closing tag** (note the `/`). - Everything between them is the element's **content**. - Opening tag + content + closing tag = an **element**. A few elements can't hold content, so they have no closing tag. These are **void elements**, like `
` (line break) and `` (image). ### Nesting Elements can contain other elements. This is called **nesting**, and tags must close in the reverse order they opened: ```html

This is very important.

This is very

``` Indenting nested elements by two spaces isn't required, but it makes the structure easy to read, and every professional team does it. ### The document skeleton Every HTML page has the same outer structure: ```html Shown in the browser tab Everything the visitor sees goes here. ``` - `` tells the browser to use modern HTML rules. - `` wraps the whole page. `lang` tells screen readers which language to speak. - `` holds information *about* the page, like the ``. - `<body>` holds everything visible. - `<main>` (inside `body`) marks the page's main content. Screen-reader users can jump straight to it. ### Whitespace Browsers collapse runs of spaces and line breaks into a single space. To start a new block of text, use a new element, not extra blank lines. ### New words - **Markup language**: a language that labels the parts of a document. - **Void element**: an element with no content and no closing tag, like `<br>`. - **Nesting**: putting elements inside other elements. - **Screen reader**: software that reads pages aloud for people who are blind or have low vision.

lessons.title: Headings and lists
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Making a list Lots of things on the web are lists: menus, top-10s, steps in a game guide. HTML has a tag for that. A **bulleted list** starts with `
    `. That stands for *unordered list*, which means the order doesn't matter. Each thing in the list goes inside `
  • `, which means *list item*: ```html
    • Pizza
    • Tacos
    • Noodles
    ``` The browser puts a bullet (•) in front of each `
  • `. Want numbers instead of bullets? Use `
      `, an *ordered list*. The browser counts 1, 2, 3 for you! ### Headings come in sizes `

      ` is the biggest heading. `

      ` is a little smaller, and is perfect for the parts of your page, like chapters in a book. ### New words - **List item** (`
    1. `): one thing in a list. - **Unordered list** (`
        `): a list with bullets. - **Ordered list** (`
          `): a list with numbers.

lessons.title: Headings, paragraphs and lists
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Structure with headings and lists ### Heading levels HTML has six heading levels, `

` through `

`. They aren't about size (CSS controls size); they describe the **outline** of your page: - `

`: the page's main title. Use one per page. - `

`: major sections. - `

`: subsections inside an `

` section, and so on. Don't skip levels (an `

` straight after an `

`). Screen-reader users often jump between headings to skim a page, and a skipped level makes it look like something is missing. ### Paragraphs `

` wraps a block of text. Remember that browsers collapse whitespace, so blank lines in your code don't create space on the page; separate paragraphs do. ### Lists | Tag | Meaning | Use it for | | --- | --- | --- | | `

    ` | Unordered list | Items where order doesn't matter (ingredients, features) | | `
      ` | Ordered list | Steps or rankings, where order matters | | `
    1. ` | List item | Each item, inside a `
        ` or `
          ` | Only `
        1. ` elements may be direct children of a `
            ` or `
              `. To **nest** a list, put the inner list *inside* an `
            1. `: ```html
              • Fruit
                • Apples
                • Kiwis
              ``` ### New words - **Outline**: the hierarchy of sections a page's headings create. - **Direct child**: an element placed immediately inside another, with nothing in between.

lessons.title: Links and pictures
lessons.learnMarkdown: ## Tags can carry extra info Some tags need more information to do their job. That extra info goes **inside the opening tag** and is called an **attribute**. An attribute has a name, an equals sign, and a value in quotes: ```html Visit NASA ``` ### Links: `` `` makes a **link**. Its `href` attribute is the web address the link goes to. The words between the tags are what people click. ### Pictures: `` ```html ``` - `src` is the picture file. - `alt` describes the picture in words. Screen readers read it aloud for people who can't see the screen, and browsers show it if the picture can't load. `` has no closing tag, because there's nothing to put between tags. > In our practice preview, picture files don't exist yet, so you'll see your alt text instead of a picture. That's alt text doing its job! ### New words - **Attribute**: extra info inside an opening tag, like `href="..."`. - **Link**: words you click to go to another page. - **Alt text**: words that describe a picture.

lessons.title: Links, images and attributes
lessons.learnMarkdown: ## Attributes, links and images ### Attributes **Attributes** configure an element. They live in the opening tag as `name="value"` pairs, separated by spaces. Some are **boolean**: present means on (``). ### Links ```html MDN Web Docs ``` The `href` can be: | Kind | Example | Goes to | | --- | --- | --- | | Absolute URL | `https://example.com/about` | A full address, usually another site | | Relative URL | `about.html`, `images/logo.png` | A file relative to the current page's folder | | Fragment | `#faq` | The element with `id="faq"` on the same page | Add `target="_blank"` to open a new tab. Pair it with `rel="noopener"` so the new page can't control yours through `window.opener`. Link text should make sense on its own: "Read the setup guide", not "click here". Screen-reader users often pull up a list of links without the sentences around them. ### Images ```html ``` - `alt` is required for meaningful images. Describe what matters, not "image of". Purely decorative images get `alt=""` so screen readers skip them. - `width` and `height` let the browser reserve space before the image loads, so the page doesn't jump. ### New words - **URL** (*Uniform Resource Locator*): the address of a page or file on the web. - **Absolute URL**: a full address including `https://`. - **Relative URL**: a path from the current page, like `images/logo.png`. - **Fragment**: the `#name` part of a URL that points to an `id` on the page.

lessons.title: Rooms of a web page
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Every page has rooms

A house has rooms with names: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom. When you hear "kitchen", you know what's inside.

Web pages have named rooms too:

- `<header>`: the top of the page, with the title or logo.
- `<nav>`: the menu of links.
- `<main>`: the main stuff the page is about. Only one per page!
- `<footer>`: the bottom, with small extra info.

These are called **semantic** tags. *Semantic* means "about meaning". They don't change how the page looks, but they tell browsers and screen readers what each part is **for**. A screen reader can jump straight to `<main>`, so nobody has to listen to the whole menu every time.

The plain `<div>` tag is a box with **no** meaning. Use the named rooms when one fits.

### New words

- **Semantic**: about meaning.
- **Screen reader**: an app that reads web pages out loud.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A tiny page split into rooms: a header at the top, the main part in the middle, and a footer at the bottom.

lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Semantic HTML and landmarks **Semantic** elements describe what content *is*, not how it looks. A `
` says nothing; a `
` says "this is navigation". | Element | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `
` | Introductory content: site title, logo, often the main nav | | `
` | A block of major navigation links | | `
` | The page's primary content. Exactly one per page, not inside header/footer/aside | | `
` | Self-contained content that would make sense on its own: a post, a card, a comment | | `
` | A thematic group of content, usually with its own heading | | `
` | Related but secondary content: sidebars, callouts | | `
` | Closing info for the page or for an article | ### Why it matters - **Accessibility.** Screen readers expose these as **landmarks**. Users jump straight to `main` or `nav` instead of listening to everything in order. - **Readable code.** `
` is much easier to match up than the fifth `
`. - **Search engines** use them to understand which part of the page matters. `
` is still fine for grouping things purely for styling, when no semantic element fits. ### New words - **Landmark**: a region of a page that assistive technology lets users jump to. - **Self-contained**: makes sense if you lifted it out and put it somewhere else.

lessons.title: Forms
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Forms that everyone can use

A `<form>` collects input and submits it. Each control's `name` becomes the key in the submitted data (`team=Bolt`).

### Input types

The `type` attribute changes the control and its built-in validation:

| `type` | Gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | A single-line text box (the default) |
| `email` | Text that must look like an email; email keyboard on phones |
| `number` | A numeric box with `min`, `max` and `step` |
| `checkbox` | An on/off choice |
| `radio` | One choice from a group: radios **sharing a `name`** are one group |

### Labels

Every control needs a label. Two ways:

```html
<!-- explicit: for matches id -->
<label for="team">Team name</label>
<input id="team" name="team">

<!-- implicit: the input sits inside the label -->
<label><input type="checkbox" name="power"> We need a power outlet</label>
```

Labels give screen readers the control's name and make small targets (checkboxes!) easier to click.

### Grouping

Wrap related controls, like a radio group, in a `<fieldset>`; its first child `<legend>` names the group. Screen readers announce "Session, group" before the options.

### Validation

`required`, `min`, `max` and `type` give you free browser validation. It's a convenience for users, never security: a server must always validate again.

### Buttons

`<button type="submit">` submits the form. A `<button>` inside a form defaults to submit, but saying so makes your intent clear.

> In the preview, submitting does nothing (forms never send data from the sandbox). The console tells you when a form would have submitted.

### New words

- **Control**: any form element a user interacts with.
- **Validation**: checking input meets rules before it's accepted.
- **Fieldset / legend**: a group of controls and its caption.

lessons.title: Pages for everyone
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Making pages everyone can use

People use the web in lots of ways. Some people can't see the screen and use a **screen reader** that reads the page out loud. Some can't use a mouse, so they press the Tab key to move around. Making pages work for everyone is called **accessibility**.

You already know the most important tricks:

1. **Alt text** on pictures, so screen readers can describe them.
2. **Labels** on form boxes, so people know what to type.
3. **Headings in order**: `<h1>` first, then `<h2>`.
4. **The `lang` attribute** on `<html>`, like `<html lang="en">`. It tells screen readers which language to speak, so English words don't get read with a Spanish voice!

> Fun fact: accessibility helps everyone. Captions help in a noisy room, and big buttons help on a bumpy bus.

### New words

- **Accessibility**: making things everyone can use, including people with disabilities.
- **`lang`**: an attribute that says which language a page is in.

lessons.title: Accessibility basics
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Accessibility basics

**Accessibility** (often written **a11y**: "a", 11 letters, "y") means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use what you build. Roughly 1 in 4 adults in the US has a disability, and the law often requires accessible sites. The standard most teams follow is **WCAG** (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines); level AA is the usual target.

### The checklist you can apply today

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `<html lang="en">` | Screen readers pick pronunciation from it |
| Meaningful `alt` on images (`alt=""` if decorative) | Non-visual users get the content |
| Heading levels in order, no skips | Users navigate and skim by headings |
| Every form control labelled | Controls get an accessible name |
| Descriptive link text, never "click here" | Links are often read as a list, out of context |
| Landmarks (`header`, `main`, `nav`, `footer`) | Users jump between regions |
| Everything works with the keyboard | Not everyone uses a mouse |
| Text contrast at least 4.5:1 | Readable for low-vision users (a CSS topic) |

### How to test

- Unplug your mouse and **Tab** through the page. Can you reach and use everything? Can you see where focus is?
- Turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver on Mac: Cmd + F5; Narrator on Windows: Ctrl + Win + Enter) and listen to your page.
- Run an automated checker such as axe DevTools or Lighthouse. Automated tools catch roughly a third of issues, so they supplement manual testing rather than replace it.

### New words

- **a11y**: short for *accessibility*. It's a shorthand, not an acronym: an "a", then 11 letters, then a "y".
- **WCAG** (*Web Content Accessibility Guidelines*): the international guidelines for accessible web content.
- **Accessible name**: what assistive tech announces for an element, such as a label's text.
